tool.name: Dart
tool.tagline: Client-optimized language with sound null safety, behind Flutter
tool.description: Dart is Google's statically typed, garbage-collected language with sound null safety, async/await, records and pattern matching. It compiles ahead of time to native code for mobile and desktop, to JavaScript or WebAssembly for the web, and runs with a JIT and hot reload during development. Learn it to build Flutter apps and command-line or server tools in one approachable language.

concepts.name: Variables, types, final and const
concepts.summary: Declare variables with var, final and const, use Dart's core types, and write a main function.
concepts.why: Every Dart program and Flutter widget starts with these declarations, and final vs const matters for performance.
concepts.body:
A Dart program starts at `void main()`. Statements end with semicolons, and `print` writes a line.

Declare variables with:

- `var name = 'Dart';` — type inferred (`String`) and fixed; you can reassign another String.
- An explicit type: `int count = 0;`.
- `final` — assigned once, at run time: `final now = DateTime.now();`.
- `const` — a **compile-time constant**: `const maxItems = 100;`. Const values are canonicalized, so two identical `const` objects are the same instance; Flutter uses this to skip rebuilding `const` widgets.

Core types: `int`, `double` (both subtypes of `num`), `String`, `bool`, plus `List`, `Set`, `Map`, `Record` and `Object`. Everything, including numbers and `null`, is an object. Conversion is explicit: `int.parse('42')`, `3.7.toInt()`, `n.toString()`.

Strings use single or double quotes; interpolate with `$name` or `${expr}`. Triple quotes make multi-line strings, and `r'...'` is a raw string.

`dynamic` turns off static checking for a variable — avoid it; use `Object?` when you truly accept anything.

Dart is **statically and soundly typed**: if a variable's static type is `int`, it really holds an int at run time. The type checker catches most mistakes before you run.
takeaways: `var` infers, `final` is set once, `const` is a compile-time constant
`/` returns double; `~/` is integer division
Interpolate with `$x` and `${expr}`
pitfalls: Using `dynamic` to silence type errors, which moves them to run time.

quiz.q: What is the difference between `final` and `const`?
options: const must be known at compile time; final is set once at run time
quiz.explain: final values are fixed after first assignment, while const values must be compile-time constants.

concepts.name: Sound null safety
concepts.summary: Use nullable types, null-aware operators, flow analysis and late variables to write code that can't hit null errors.
concepts.why: Null safety removes a whole class of crashes, and every Dart and Flutter API is written with it.
concepts.body:
In Dart 3, types are **non-nullable** by default: a `String` can never be `null`. Add `?` to allow it: `String? nickname;`. Nullable variables start as `null`; non-nullable locals must be assigned before use.

Null-aware operators:

- `a ?? b` — `a` unless it is null, then `b`.
- `x ??= value` — assign only if `x` is null.
- `user?.name` — null if `user` is null, otherwise the property.
- `value!` — assert non-null; throws if it is null. Use sparingly.

**Flow analysis** promotes types: after `if (name != null)`, `name` is treated as `String` inside the block. The same happens after an early `return` or `throw`. Promotion only works for local variables and private final fields, because a public field or getter could return something different the next time.

`late` declares a non-nullable variable that is initialized later: `late final String token;`. Reading it before assignment throws. `late` with an initializer makes it lazy: the expression runs on first access.

Since Dart 3.8, collection literals support **null-aware elements**: `[?maybeItem]` adds the item only if it is non-null.

The guarantee is **sound**: once your program and its dependencies are null-safe, a non-nullable expression can never evaluate to null at run time.
takeaways: Types are non-nullable unless marked `?`
Prefer `??`, `?.` and null checks over `!`
Flow analysis promotes local variables after a null check
pitfalls: Expecting a class field to promote after `if (field != null)` — copy it to a local first.

quiz.q: Why doesn't `if (this.name != null) print(this.name.length);` compile when `name` is a public non-final `String?` field?
options: Fields aren't promoted because their value could change between the check and the use
this is not allowed in Dart
quiz.explain: Only locals and private final fields are promoted; a public field could return a different value on the next read.

concepts.name: Operators and control flow
concepts.summary: Branch with if, switch expressions and the conditional operator, and loop with for, for-in and while.
concepts.why: These are the everyday building blocks, and Dart 3's switch expressions replace many if/else chains.
concepts.body:
`if` / `else if` / `else` work as in C-like languages; the condition must be a `bool` — Dart has no truthiness. The conditional operator `cond ? a : b` picks a value.

Loops:

- `for (var i = 0; i < n; i++)` — classic counter loop; each iteration gets a fresh `i`, so closures capture the right value.
- `for (final item in items)` — iterate any `Iterable`.
- `while` and `do { } while`.
- `break` and `continue`, with labels for nested loops.

`switch` in Dart 3 matches **patterns**. Cases don't fall through when they have a body, so no `break` is needed. Empty cases share the next body.

A **switch expression** produces a value:

```dart
final label = switch (code) {
  200 => 'ok',
  404 => 'not found',
  >= 500 => 'server error',
  _ => 'other',
};
```

Each case is `pattern => expression`, separated by commas; `_` is the wildcard. Switch expressions must be **exhaustive**, which the compiler checks.

Useful operators: `~/` (integer division), `%` (remainder), `is` and `is!` (type tests, which also promote), `as` (cast), and the cascade `..` (call several members on the same object).
takeaways: Conditions must be real bools
Switch expressions `pattern => value` must be exhaustive
`..` cascades call several members on one object
pitfalls: Writing `case 1: case 2:` with bodies in Dart 2 style and expecting fall-through.

quiz.q: What is `switch (7) { > 5 => 'big', _ => 'small' }`?
quiz.explain: The relational pattern > 5 matches 7, so the first case's value is produced.

concepts.name: Functions and parameters
concepts.summary: Write functions with positional, optional and named parameters, arrow syntax and closures.
concepts.why: Named parameters are everywhere in Flutter, and functions as values drive callbacks and collection methods.
concepts.body:
A function declares its return type, name and parameters: `int add(int a, int b) { return a + b; }`. For a single expression, use **arrow syntax**: `int add(int a, int b) => a + b;`.

Parameter kinds:

- **Required positional**: `f(int a)`.
- **Optional positional** in brackets: `f(int a, [int b = 0])`.
- **Named** in braces: `f({required String name, int age = 0})`. Callers write `f(name: 'Ana')`. Named parameters are optional unless marked `required`; optional ones need a default or a nullable type.

You can't mix optional positional and named parameters in the same function. Flutter APIs use named parameters almost everywhere because they read clearly: `Padding(padding: ..., child: ...)`.

Functions are objects. You can assign them to variables, pass them as arguments and return them. Their types are written like `int Function(int, int)`. Anonymous functions look like `(x) => x * 2` or `(x) { ... }`.

A function that refers to variables from its surrounding scope is a **closure**; it keeps those variables alive and sees later changes.

`typedef Compare = int Function(String a, String b);` gives a function type a name. Top-level functions, static methods and instance methods (tear-offs like `list.add`) can all be passed where a function is expected.
takeaways: Named params `{...}` are optional unless `required`
`=>` is shorthand for a one-expression body
Functions are values; closures capture variables
pitfalls: Forgetting `required` on a non-nullable named parameter without a default, which is a compile error.

quiz.q: Given `void f(int a, {int b = 1})`, which call is valid?
quiz.explain: a is a required positional argument and b is named, so it must be passed as b: 2.

concepts.name: Lists, sets and maps
concepts.summary: Use List, Set and Map literals, collection if and for, and the spread operator.
concepts.why: Collections hold almost all app data, and collection-if/for is how Flutter builds lists of widgets.
concepts.body:
Dart's core collections:

- `List<T>` — ordered, zero-indexed: `var nums = [1, 2, 3];`.
- `Set<T>` — unique items: `var tags = {'dart', 'flutter'};`.
- `Map<K, V>` — key/value pairs: `var ages = {'ana': 31, 'bo': 25};`.

An empty `{}` is a **Map**; write `<String>{}` for an empty Set. Type arguments can be explicit: `<int>[]`.

Lists support `add`, `addAll`, `insert`, `removeAt`, `length`, `first`, `last`, `contains`, `indexOf`, `sort`. Out-of-range indexing throws a `RangeError`. Map lookup `ages['zoe']` returns `null` (the value type becomes nullable); use `containsKey`, `putIfAbsent` or `update(key, f, ifAbsent: ...)`. Iterate maps with `for (final MapEntry(:key, :value) in ages.entries)` or `ages.forEach`.

Collection literals have special syntax:

- **Spread**: `[...a, ...b]`, and null-aware `...?maybeList`.
- **Collection if**: `[ 'home', if (loggedIn) 'profile' ]`.
- **Collection for**: `[for (final n in nums) n * n]`.

This lets Flutter build widget lists declaratively: `children: [Header(), if (showBanner) Banner(), for (final m in messages) Tile(m)]`.

Collections are mutable unless created `const` or with `List.unmodifiable`. A `final` variable can still have its list contents changed; only reassignment is blocked.
takeaways: `[]` List, `{a, b}` Set, `{k: v}` Map; `{}` alone is a Map
Collection if/for and spread `...` build lists declaratively
Map lookup returns a nullable value
pitfalls: Declaring `var s = {};` expecting a Set and getting a `Map<dynamic, dynamic>`.

quiz.q: What does `[1, if (false) 2, for (var i in [3, 4]) i * 2]` produce?
quiz.explain: The if element contributes nothing when false, and the for element adds 6 and 8.

concepts.name: Classes and constructors
concepts.summary: Define classes with fields, getters, methods and the many constructor forms: initializing formals, named, const and factory.
concepts.why: Everything in Flutter is a class, and widget classes rely on const and named constructors.
concepts.body:
A class declares fields, constructors and methods. Every non-nullable field must be initialized before the constructor body runs.

Constructor forms:

- **Initializing formals**: `Point(this.x, this.y);` assigns parameters directly to fields. Named: `Person({required this.name, this.age = 0});`.
- **Initializer list** after `:` runs before the body: `Rect(double w) : width = w, height = w * 2;`. It can also hold `assert`s.
- **Named constructors** give alternatives: `Point.origin() : x = 0, y = 0;`.
- **Redirecting**: `Point.onX(double x) : this(x, 0);`.
- **const constructors** for immutable classes (all fields `final`): `const Point(this.x, this.y);`. Calling with `const Point(1, 2)` creates a canonical compile-time constant.
- **factory constructors** may return an existing instance or a subtype, e.g. from a cache or `fromJson`.

**Getters and setters** look like fields: `double get area => width * height;`. Fields are implicitly given getters (and setters if not final), so you can later replace a field with a getter without changing callers.

Privacy is per **library** (file), not per class: names starting with `_` are private to the file.

Override `toString`, `==` and `hashCode` for value-like classes; otherwise `==` compares identity. Dart has no `new` requirement — just call `Point(1, 2)`.
takeaways: `this.x` parameters and initializer lists set final fields
Named, const and factory constructors cover most creation needs
`_name` is private to the library (file), not the class
pitfalls: Overriding `==` without also overriding `hashCode`, which breaks Sets and Maps.

quiz.q: Where is a member named `_cache` visible?
quiz.explain: Dart privacy is library-level: underscore names are visible throughout the declaring file.

concepts.name: Iterables and collection methods
concepts.summary: Transform data with map, where, fold, expand and any, and understand that Iterable operations are lazy.
concepts.why: Most data shaping in Dart and Flutter is a chain of iterable methods, and laziness explains surprising behavior.
concepts.body:
`List` and `Set` are `Iterable`s, as are `map.keys`, `map.values` and `map.entries`. `Iterable` offers a rich set of methods that take functions:

- `map(f)` — transform each element.
- `where(test)` — keep elements matching a condition; `whereType<T>()` filters by type.
- `expand(f)` — map each element to several and flatten.
- `fold(initial, combine)` and `reduce(combine)` — combine into one value.
- `any`, `every`, `contains`, `firstWhere(test, orElse: ...)`.
- `take`, `skip`, `takeWhile`, `skipWhile`.
- `join(', ')`, `toList()`, `toSet()`.

Key fact: `map`, `where`, `expand` and friends are **lazy**. They return an `Iterable` view that runs the function each time it is iterated. If you iterate twice, the function runs twice; if you never iterate, it never runs. Call `.toList()` when you need a concrete, reusable result or a `List` type (Flutter's `children` requires a `List<Widget>`).

`package:collection` adds helpers such as `firstWhereOrNull`, `groupBy`, `sortedBy` and deep equality. In Dart 3 the core library also has `firstOrNull`, `lastOrNull` and `indexed` (pairs of index and element as records).

`sort` mutates the list in place and returns `void`, so it can't be chained; copy first if you need the original order.
takeaways: `map`/`where` are lazy views — call `toList()` to materialize
`fold` combines with an initial value; `reduce` needs a non-empty iterable
`sort` mutates in place and returns void
pitfalls: Passing `items.map(...)` where a `List` is required, or iterating an expensive lazy chain many times.

quiz.q: `final it = [1, 2, 3].map(f);` — how many times has `f` run after this line alone?
options: It depends on the list type
quiz.explain: map is lazy: f only runs when the resulting Iterable is iterated.

concepts.name: Exceptions and error handling
concepts.summary: Throw and catch exceptions with try, on, catch and finally, and know when to use Exception vs Error.
concepts.why: Parsing, I/O and network calls all throw, and catching the right type keeps apps from crashing or hiding bugs.
takeaways: Throw `Exception`s for recoverable problems; `Error`s mean bugs
`on Type catch (e, s)` catches selectively; `rethrow` passes it on
Prefer non-throwing variants like `tryParse` for expected bad input
pitfalls: A bare `catch (e)` that swallows everything, including real bugs.

quiz.q: Which clause catches only FormatException and gives access to it?
quiz.explain: Dart uses on Type to filter and catch (e) to bind the exception object.

concepts.name: Inheritance, abstract classes and interfaces
concepts.summary: Extend classes, override members, write abstract classes, and implement any class as an interface.
concepts.why: Flutter's widget hierarchy and most APIs depend on extends and implements, and Dart treats them differently from Java.
concepts.body:
`class Dog extends Animal` inherits Animal's fields and methods. Override members with the `@override` annotation and call the parent with `super.method()`. Constructors aren't inherited; a subclass constructor forwards with `super(...)`, or more concisely with **super parameters**: `Dog(super.name);`.

An **abstract class** can't be instantiated and can declare methods without bodies, which concrete subclasses must implement:

```dart
abstract class Shape {
  double get area;           // abstract getter
  String describe() => 'Shape with area $area';
}
```

Dart has no separate `interface` keyword in the Java sense: **every class implicitly defines an interface** consisting of its public members. `class MockClient implements HttpClient` must provide all of them itself — nothing is inherited. A class can `extends` only one class but `implements` many.

Use `extends` to reuse implementation and `implements` to promise a contract (common for test doubles). Since Dart 3, class modifiers such as `interface`, `base` and `final` let library authors restrict which of these is allowed outside their library.

`Object` is the root of all non-nullable types. `toString`, `==`, `hashCode` and `noSuchMethod` come from it.

Type tests with `is` promote: `if (shape is Circle) print(shape.radius);`. Covariance of overridden parameters requires the `covariant` keyword.
takeaways: `extends` inherits code from one superclass
Every class is an implicit interface; `implements` copies only the contract
Abstract classes declare members subclasses must provide
pitfalls: Using `implements` and expecting to inherit method bodies.

quiz.q: `class B implements A` where A has a concrete method `hello()`. What must B do?
quiz.explain: implements takes only A's interface, so B must implement every member itself.

concepts.name: Mixins
concepts.summary: Reuse behavior across unrelated classes with mixin declarations and the with clause.
concepts.why: Flutter uses mixins heavily, such as TickerProviderStateMixin and ChangeNotifier, and they solve multiple-inheritance needs.
takeaways: `with A, B` layers mixins left to right; later ones override earlier ones
`mixin M on Base` restricts use and allows `super` calls
Mixins have no constructors; declare with `mixin` or `mixin class`
pitfalls: Relying on mixin order without realizing a later mixin silently overrides an earlier method.

quiz.q: `class C extends Base with A, B` and both A and B override `run()`, calling super. Which runs first when calling `C().run()`?
options: B's run(), which calls A's via super
quiz.explain: Mixins are linearized left to right, so B is the outermost layer and its super is A.

concepts.name: Enhanced enums
concepts.summary: Declare enums with fields, constructors, methods and interfaces, and switch over them exhaustively.
concepts.why: Enums model fixed sets like states and themes, and exhaustive switches catch missed cases at compile time.
takeaways: Enums can have final fields, a const constructor, methods and interfaces
Switches over enums are exhaustive without `default`
Use `name` and `values.byName` for serialization
pitfalls: Adding `_ =>` to every enum switch, which hides newly added values.

quiz.q: What must an enhanced enum's constructor be?
quiz.explain: Enum values are compile-time constants, so the generative constructor must be const.

concepts.name: Generics
concepts.summary: Write generic classes and functions, bound type parameters with extends, and understand reified generics.
concepts.why: Typed collections, Futures and Flutter widgets like ValueListenableBuilder<T> are generic, and you'll write your own.
takeaways: Type parameters keep code reusable and type-safe
`T extends Bound` lets you call the bound's members
Generics are reified: `is List<int>` is checked at run time
pitfalls: Relying on covariance and adding a wider type to a narrower list, which throws at run time.

quiz.q: What is printed by `Object x = <int>[]; print(x is List<String>);`?
quiz.explain: Dart keeps type arguments at run time, so a List<int> is not a List<String>.

concepts.name: Futures and async/await
concepts.summary: Work with Future, async and await, handle errors, and run independent futures in parallel with Future.wait.
concepts.why: Every network call, file read and database query in Dart and Flutter returns a Future.
concepts.body:
A **`Future<T>`** represents a value (or error) that will be available later. Functions that do I/O return futures instead of blocking, because Dart runs your code on a single thread per isolate.

Mark a function `async` and use `await` to wait for a future without blocking:

```dart
Future<User> loadUser(int id) async {
  final json = await api.get('/users/$id');
  return User.fromJson(json);
}
```

An `async` function always returns a `Future`, even if the body returns a plain value. Use `Future<void>` when nothing is returned. Errors from awaited futures are thrown at the `await`, so ordinary `try`/`catch`/`finally` works.

Important behaviors:

- An `async` function runs synchronously until its first `await`, then returns the future to its caller.
- Sequential `await`s run one after another. For independent work, start the futures first and wait together: `await Future.wait([a(), b()])`, or with records `final (u, p) = await (loadUser(), loadPosts()).wait;`.
- `.timeout(Duration(...))` fails a slow future with a `TimeoutException`.
- A future you forget to await runs anyway, but its errors become uncaught. Enable the `unawaited_futures` lint and wrap intentional fire-and-forget calls in `unawaited(...)`.

`Future.delayed`, `Future.value` and `Completer` create futures yourself; the latter bridges callback-based APIs.
takeaways: `async` functions return a Future; `await` unwraps it
Start independent futures together and wait with `Future.wait` or `(a, b).wait`
Errors surface at `await` and are caught with try/catch
pitfalls: Forgetting `await`, so errors go uncaught and code runs out of order.

quiz.q: `final x = loadUser();` inside an async function, without await. What is x?
quiz.explain: Without await you get the Future itself, not its eventual value.

concepts.name: Records and patterns
concepts.summary: Return multiple values with records, and destructure and match data with patterns in variables, switch and if-case.
concepts.why: Records and patterns are Dart 3's biggest additions and make JSON handling and state matching concise and safe.
concepts.body:
A **record** is an anonymous, immutable, fixed-size aggregate: `(1, 'a')` or with named fields `(name: 'Ana', age: 31)`. Its type is written the same way: `(int, String)` or `({String name, int age})`. Positional fields are read with `$1`, `$2`; named ones by name. Records have structural `==` and `hashCode`, so they're great for returning several values:

```dart
(double, double) minMax(List<double> xs) => (xs.reduce(min), xs.reduce(max));
final (lo, hi) = minMax(data);
```

**Patterns** describe the shape of a value and destructure it. They appear in:

- Variable declarations: `final (lo, hi) = ...;`, `var {'name': name} = json;`.
- `switch` statements and expressions.
- `if (value case pattern)` — match and bind in a condition.
- `for` loops: `for (final (i, x) in list.indexed)`.

Pattern kinds include constants, relational (`> 0`), logical (`||`, `&&`), records, lists (`[first, ...rest]`), maps (`{'id': int id}`), objects (`Point(x: 0, :var y)`), wildcards `_`, casts and null checks (`var x?`).

Map and list patterns check types as they bind, which makes validating untyped JSON clean: `if (json case {'name': String name, 'age': int age}) ...` only matches when both keys exist with the right types. A `when` clause adds a guard: `case (var a, var b) when a > b:`.
takeaways: Records `(a, b)` / `(name: x)` bundle values with structural equality
Patterns destructure in declarations, switch, if-case and for
Map/list patterns type-check while binding — ideal for JSON
pitfalls: Matching JSON numbers with `int` when the server may send `1.0`; use `num` and convert.

quiz.q: Does `{'id': int id}` match the map `{'id': 7, 'extra': true}`?
options: No, extra keys make map patterns fail
Yes, map patterns ignore keys they don't mention
quiz.explain: Map patterns only check the listed keys; unmentioned keys are allowed.

concepts.name: Libraries, packages and pub
concepts.summary: Organize code into libraries, import with prefixes and show/hide, and manage dependencies with pubspec.yaml and dart pub.
concepts.why: Real projects depend on packages from pub.dev and are split into libraries with clear public APIs.
concepts.body:
Every Dart file is a **library**. `import` brings in another library's public names:

- `import 'dart:math';` — core libraries.
- `import 'package:http/http.dart' as http;` — a package, with a **prefix** to avoid name clashes.
- `import 'src/utils.dart';` — a relative path within your package.
- `show` and `hide` limit which names are imported: `import 'dart:math' show max, pi;`.

Privacy is per library: `_names` are private to the file. Big libraries can be split with `part`/`part of`, but most code just uses separate libraries. A package's public API lives in `lib/`, with implementation in `lib/src/` and a top-level file that `export`s what users should see.

A **package** is a directory with a `pubspec.yaml` declaring its name, SDK constraint (`environment: sdk: ^3.9.0`), `dependencies` and `dev_dependencies`. Version constraints use caret syntax: `http: ^1.2.0` means at least 1.2.0 but below 2.0.0.

Commands:

- `dart create my_app` — new project.
- `dart pub add http` / `dart pub add --dev test` — add dependencies.
- `dart pub get` — resolve and download; writes `pubspec.lock` (commit it for apps).
- `dart pub outdated` and `dart pub upgrade`.
- `dart run`, `dart analyze`, `dart format`, `dart fix --apply`.

`analysis_options.yaml` configures the analyzer; `package:lints` provides recommended rules.
concepts.code:
# pubspec.yaml
name: weather_cli
description: A tiny command-line weather client.
version: 1.0.0
environment:
  sdk: ^3.9.0

dependencies:
  http: ^1.2.0
  args: ^2.5.0

dev_dependencies:
  lints: ^5.0.0
  test: ^1.25.0

# lib/weather_cli.dart (the package's public API):
#   export 'src/client.dart' show WeatherClient;
# bin/main.dart:
#   import 'package:weather_cli/weather_cli.dart';
#   import 'package:http/http.dart' as http;
#   import 'dart:math' show max;
# Commands: dart pub get · dart run · dart analyze · dart test
takeaways: `import ... as p` and `show`/`hide` control names
Public API in `lib/`, internals in `lib/src/`, re-exported with `export`
`^1.2.0` allows compatible updates below 2.0.0
pitfalls: Importing another package's `src/` files directly — they're private implementation details.

quiz.q: What versions does the constraint `http: ^1.2.0` allow?
quiz.explain: Caret syntax allows any version compatible under semantic versioning, up to the next major.

concepts.name: Streams
concepts.summary: Consume and create streams with await for, listen, async* generators and StreamController, and know single vs broadcast.
concepts.why: Streams model repeated async events such as user input, sockets, database watches and Flutter's StreamBuilder.
concepts.body:
A **`Stream<T>`** delivers a sequence of asynchronous events — data, errors, and a final done. Where a `Future` gives one value, a stream gives many.

Consuming:

- `await for (final event in stream) { ... }` inside an `async` function, with `try`/`catch` for errors. The loop ends when the stream closes.
- `stream.listen(onData, onError: ..., onDone: ...)` returns a `StreamSubscription` you can `pause`, `resume` and must `cancel()` when done (for example in a Flutter `dispose`).

Streams have iterable-like transformers: `map`, `where`, `take`, `skip`, `distinct`, `asyncMap`, `expand`, plus `first`, `toList()` and `fold` that return futures.

Producing:

- An **`async*` generator** function with `yield` (and `yield*` to forward another stream). It's lazy: the body starts when someone listens and pauses when the listener pauses.
- A **`StreamController`** when events come from elsewhere: `controller.add(x)`, `addError`, `close()`, and expose `controller.stream`.

**Single-subscription** streams (the default, e.g. file reads) allow exactly one listener and buffer events until it subscribes. **Broadcast** streams (`StreamController.broadcast()`, `asBroadcastStream()`) allow many listeners but drop events no one is listening to. Listening twice to a single-subscription stream throws a `StateError`.

For advanced operators (debounce, combineLatest), the `rxdart` and `stream_transform` packages are common.
takeaways: Consume with `await for` or `listen`, and cancel subscriptions
Produce with `async*`/`yield` or a StreamController
Single-subscription = one listener; broadcast = many, no buffering
pitfalls: Never cancelling a `listen` subscription, leaking memory and work after a widget is gone.

quiz.q: What happens if you call listen twice on a default (single-subscription) StreamController's stream?
options: The first listener is replaced silently
The second listen throws a StateError
quiz.explain: Single-subscription streams allow exactly one listener; use broadcast for several.

concepts.name: Sealed classes and class modifiers
concepts.summary: Model closed type hierarchies with sealed classes for exhaustive switches, and control APIs with base, interface, final and mixin modifiers.
concepts.why: Sealed hierarchies plus pattern matching give algebraic data types, ideal for states, results and events.
concepts.body:
A **`sealed`** class is implicitly abstract and can only be extended or implemented **within its own library**. Because the compiler knows every direct subtype, a `switch` over a sealed type is checked for **exhaustiveness**:

```dart
sealed class Result<T> {}
class Ok<T> extends Result<T> { Ok(this.value); final T value; }
class Err<T> extends Result<T> { Err(this.error); final Object error; }
```

`switch (r) { Ok(:final value) => ..., Err(:final error) => ... }` needs no default, and adding a new subclass turns every incomplete switch into a compile error. This is the Dart 3 way to model UI states (`Loading`, `Loaded`, `Failed`), API results and events.

Dart 3 also adds modifiers that control how classes may be used **outside** their library:

- `base` — can be extended but not implemented; subclasses must be `base`, `final` or `sealed`. Guarantees your constructor and private members run.
- `interface` — can be implemented but not extended.
- `final` — neither extended nor implemented outside the library.
- `abstract` — can't be instantiated; combine with the others (`abstract interface class` is a pure interface).
- `mixin class` — usable as both a class and a mixin.

Inside the declaring library these restrictions don't apply. Use them when publishing packages to keep the freedom to evolve classes without breaking users.
takeaways: `sealed` = closed set of subtypes in one library, enabling exhaustive switches
Object patterns like `Loaded(:final items)` destructure fields
`base`, `interface`, `final` restrict extends/implements outside the library
pitfalls: Splitting a sealed hierarchy across files without `part`, which isn't allowed — subtypes must be in the same library.

quiz.q: Why can a switch over a sealed class omit a default case?
options: The compiler knows all direct subtypes and checks they are all handled
Defaults are never needed in Dart 3
quiz.explain: All direct subtypes must be in the same library, so the compiler can verify exhaustiveness.

concepts.name: Extension methods and extension types
concepts.summary: Add methods to existing types with extensions, and create zero-cost wrapper types with extension types.
concepts.why: Extensions keep helper code readable, and extension types give type safety for IDs and interop without allocation.
takeaways: Extensions add members, resolved by static type
Extension types are compile-time-only wrappers with zero run-time cost
Use extension types for typed IDs and interop, not for security
pitfalls: Calling an extension method on a `dynamic` value and getting a NoSuchMethodError.

quiz.q: At run time, what is a value of `extension type UserId(int value)`?
options: A UserId object wrapping an int
quiz.explain: Extension types are erased; at run time the representation value itself is used.

concepts.name: Testing and static analysis
concepts.summary: Write unit tests with package:test, use groups, setUp and matchers, test async code, and enforce lints with the analyzer.
concepts.why: Tests and lints are what keep a Dart codebase or Flutter app maintainable as it grows.
concepts.body:
`package:test` is the standard test framework (Flutter's `flutter_test` builds on it). Tests live in `test/` in files ending `_test.dart`, and run with `dart test`.

```dart
test('adds', () => expect(add(1, 2), 3));
```

Structure with `group('name', () { ... })`, and share fixtures with `setUp` / `tearDown` (per test) and `setUpAll` / `tearDownAll`.

`expect(actual, matcher)` accepts values or **matchers**: `equals`, `isTrue`, `isNull`, `contains`, `hasLength`, `closeTo(3.14, 0.01)`, `isA<FormatException>()`, `throwsA(...)`, `throwsArgumentError`, `completion(...)` for futures and `emitsInOrder([...])` for streams.

Async tests just return a future: mark the body `async` and `await`. For code that throws, wrap the call: `expect(() => parse('x'), throwsFormatException)`.

Run a subset with `dart test --name 'parser'` or a single file. Use `package:mocktail` or `mockito` for fakes, though a hand-written class that `implements` the dependency is often simpler.

**Static analysis** catches problems without running code: `dart analyze` reports errors, warnings and lints configured in `analysis_options.yaml`. Include `package:lints/recommended.yaml` (or `flutter_lints`) and add rules like `unawaited_futures` and `prefer_final_locals`. `dart format` gives one canonical style, and `dart fix --apply` auto-applies many suggestions. Run all three in CI.
takeaways: `test`, `group`, `setUp` and `expect` with matchers
Async tests are `async` functions; wrap throwing calls in a closure
Run `dart analyze`, `dart format` and tests in CI
pitfalls: Writing `expect(parse('x'), throwsA(...))` without the `() =>` closure, so the exception is thrown before expect sees it.

quiz.q: Why must you write `expect(() => f(), throwsStateError)` rather than `expect(f(), throwsStateError)`?
options: The closure makes the test async
Without the closure, f() throws before expect runs, failing the test
It is only a style preference
quiz.explain: expect needs to call the function itself so it can catch and check the exception.

concepts.name: The event loop and microtasks
concepts.summary: Understand Dart's single-threaded event loop, the microtask and event queues, and the exact ordering of async code.
concepts.why: Ordering bugs, frozen UIs and flaky tests come from misunderstanding when async callbacks actually run.
concepts.body:
Each isolate runs one thread with an **event loop** and two queues:

- The **microtask queue** — short internal follow-ups: `scheduleMicrotask`, `Future.microtask`, and completions of already-completed futures and `await` continuations.
- The **event queue** — external events: timers (`Future.delayed`, `Timer`, `Future(...)`), I/O, user input, messages from other isolates, and in Flutter, frame callbacks.

The loop runs the current synchronous code to completion, then **drains the entire microtask queue**, then takes one event, and repeats. So:

- Synchronous code is never interrupted. A long loop on the main isolate freezes the UI because no events (including frames) can run.
- Microtasks always run before the next timer, even `Future.delayed(Duration.zero)`.
- Too many microtasks starve the event queue, delaying I/O and frames.

An `async` function runs synchronously up to its first `await`. When the awaited future completes, the rest of the function is scheduled as a microtask. `await` on a non-future value still yields to the microtask queue.

`Future(() => ...)` schedules on the event queue; `Future.value(x).then(...)` and `Future.sync` run the callback in a microtask or immediately. **Zones** (`runZonedGuarded`) carry context across async gaps — Flutter uses them to catch uncaught async errors.

For heavy CPU work, async doesn't help; move it to another isolate.
takeaways: Sync code runs to completion; then all microtasks; then one event
`await` continuations and `then` on completed futures are microtasks
Timers and `Future()` go on the event queue, after all microtasks
pitfalls: Doing heavy synchronous work in an async function and expecting it not to block the UI.

quiz.q: Which prints first: a `Future.delayed(Duration.zero, ...)` callback or a `scheduleMicrotask` callback scheduled after it?
options: The delayed callback, because it was scheduled first
The microtask, because the microtask queue drains before any event
quiz.explain: The event loop always empties the microtask queue before taking the next event such as a timer.

concepts.name: Isolates and parallelism
concepts.summary: Run CPU-heavy work in parallel with Isolate.run, communicate with ports, and know what can be sent between isolates.
concepts.why: Isolates are Dart's only way to use multiple cores and keep a Flutter UI at 60+ fps during heavy work.
concepts.body:
Dart code runs in **isolates**: each has its own memory heap and event loop, and isolates **share no mutable state**. That's why Dart needs no locks — and why parallelism requires message passing.

The simplest API is **`Isolate.run`** (Dart 2.19+):

```dart
final result = await Isolate.run(() => parseHugeJson(text));
```

It spawns an isolate, runs the function, returns its result and shuts the isolate down. Flutter's `compute(fn, arg)` is a wrapper around the same idea. Use it for work that takes more than a few milliseconds: JSON decoding of large payloads, image processing, encryption, search indexing.

For long-lived workers, use `Isolate.spawn` with a **`SendPort`/`ReceivePort`** pair: the worker sends back its own `SendPort`, and both sides exchange messages.

What can be sent: most objects are **copied** (deep copy), including lists, maps, records and instances of your classes. Exceptions: objects holding native resources such as `Socket`, `ReceivePort` or `DynamicLibrary` can't be sent. Closures can be sent only if what they capture is sendable — capturing a big object by accident copies it too. `Isolate.exit` transfers the result without copying when ending a worker; `TransferableTypedData` moves byte buffers cheaply.

Isolates spawned from the same isolate group share code and start quickly (tens of microseconds to milliseconds). On the web, isolates aren't available in the same form; use web workers.
takeaways: Isolates have separate heaps and communicate only by messages
`Isolate.run` (or Flutter's `compute`) offloads one CPU-heavy task
Messages are copied; native resources can't be sent
pitfalls: Capturing a large object in the closure passed to `Isolate.run`, silently copying it to the new isolate.

quiz.q: Why doesn't Dart need mutexes for ordinary objects shared between isolates?
options: Isolates don't share mutable memory; data is copied or transferred in messages
The VM locks every object automatically
Only one isolate runs at a time
quiz.explain: Each isolate has its own heap, so there is no shared mutable state to protect.

concepts.name: Compilation, runtime and the type system
concepts.summary: Know how Dart compiles (JIT, AOT, JS, Wasm), what soundness guarantees at run time, and how tree shaking and the GC affect apps.
concepts.why: Expert decisions about startup time, binary size, web targets and generated code depend on how the toolchain works.
concepts.body:
Dart has several compilation targets:

- **JIT** (`dart run`, Flutter debug): the VM compiles on the fly, enabling **hot reload** — new code is injected into the running isolate while its heap is kept.
- **AOT** (`dart compile exe`, Flutter release): ahead-of-time compiled machine code with a small runtime, fast startup and no JIT. Reflection via `dart:mirrors` is unavailable, which is why Dart relies on code generation (`build_runner` with generators such as `json_serializable`).
- **Web**: `dart compile js` (dart2js, optimized JavaScript) and `dart compile wasm` (WasmGC, used by Flutter web's `--wasm` builds).

AOT and web builds perform **tree shaking**: unreachable code is removed, so binary size depends on what you actually call.

The type system is **sound**: static types are guaranteed at run time, enforced by the compiler plus a few run-time checks — explicit casts (`as`), covariant generics, and covariant parameters. Soundness lets AOT compilers trust types to unbox numbers, devirtualize calls and skip null checks.

Memory is managed by a **generational garbage collector**: a fast scavenger for the young generation (most objects die young) and a concurrent mark-sweep/compact for the old generation. Short-lived allocations are cheap, but in Flutter large allocations per frame still cause GC pauses; reuse buffers in hot paths.

`dart:ffi` calls C directly from native targets, with `NativeFinalizer` tying C resource lifetimes to Dart objects.
concepts.code:
# Development: JIT with fast edit/run cycles and hot reload in Flutter
dart run bin/main.dart

# Native self-contained executable (AOT, tree-shaken)
dart compile exe bin/main.dart -o build/tool
./build/tool

# Smaller AOT snapshot run by dartaotruntime
dart compile aot-snapshot bin/main.dart

# Web targets
dart compile js -O2 web/main.dart -o build/main.js
dart compile wasm web/main.dart -o build/main.wasm

# Generate code instead of reflection (e.g. json_serializable)
dart run build_runner build --delete-conflicting-outputs
takeaways: JIT enables hot reload; AOT gives fast startup and no reflection
Soundness lets compilers trust static types for optimization
Generational GC makes short-lived objects cheap, but avoid big per-frame allocations
pitfalls: Expecting `dart:mirrors` reflection to work in Flutter or AOT builds — use code generation.

quiz.q: Why do Dart AOT targets rely on code generation (e.g. json_serializable) instead of reflection?
options: Generated code runs only on the web
dart:mirrors isn't available in AOT/Flutter, and generated code allows tree shaking
quiz.explain: Mirrors would defeat tree shaking and aren't supported by the AOT toolchains, so code is generated at build time.
